title: Music everywhere: ball games, prize fights and his uncle
summary: Allen asks about bands at ball games and prize fights; Hug describes his vaudeville comedian uncle.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Can I ask a silly question?

Maybe, but, you know, it isn't just the music that interests me. It's also the people and the way the people like music and, you know, what music did for them. And I was thinking once, somebody like Sal Gutierrez, one of those people from up around Coliseum Square showed me a picture once. I think you were playing baseball. Would it have been?
Different people from the neighborhood. Baseball.
We used to play ball out on Coliseum Square there.
At ball games, did you ever hear a band?
A band? Oh, yeah. They had bands. But I can't tell you who it was.
Yeah. I mean, it just was something there.
Everywhere you went. How did it work?

The prize fights, when they used to have fights, you know, they used to have a wagon or a truck, and they had bands playing, advertising the fights, and some good bands. So it was always good music. But you see, people, always in New Orleans here, people just took things for granted. I mean, you know, they didn't think that this was ever going to be something historic. At the time that they were playing in wagons and trucks advertising the prize fights, you don't think that they ever thought that this would be part of a New Orleans jazz figure, you know. I mean, it was just the regular thing that was happening here, that's all.
Well, your uncle was in the circus?
My uncle was in vaudeville. No, he wasn't in circus. He was a vaudeville comedian. He was a straight man, and he had a black-faced comedian that used to do the comedy work with him, you know.
And he did give me a lot of encouragement.
